ap_statistics-m01.stem: A researcher wants to study how much time students at the high schools of a school district spend using the school library each week. Which of the following is a valid investigative question that requires a statistical investigation?

options.text: How much time did Maria, a junior at one of the high schools, spend in the school library last Tuesday?
options.why: Asks about one individual, so there is no population and no variability to investigate.

options.text: How many students are enrolled at the largest high school in the district this year?
options.why: Asks for a single count that can be looked up, so no variability in data is anticipated and no statistical investigation is needed.

options.text: What proportion of students at the district's high schools spend more than two hours per week using the school library?
options.why: Anticipates variability among the individuals, names the population and can be answered by collecting and analyzing data.

options.text: Should the district spend more money on its school libraries?
options.why: Asks for an opinion or a value judgment that data collection and analysis cannot settle.

blueprint.subject: ap_statistics
blueprint.concept: Recognize a valid investigative question that requires a statistical investigation
student_thinking: Check whether the question anticipates variability among individuals rather than asking for one fixed value
Check that the question names a population and can be answered by collecting and analyzing data, not by opinion

key_conditions.condition: a valid investigative question anticipates variability, refers to a population and can be answered with data
key_conditions.evidence: three options each lack exactly one of these three properties

misconceptions.description: asks for a count or fact that can be looked up
asks about one person
asks for an opinion

verification.independent_path: each option is generated from a table of three properties (variability, population, answerable with data) and exactly one option has all three

ap_statistics-m02.stem: A random sample of $300$ households in a town was surveyed, and the variables in the table shown were recorded for each individual. Which of the following investigative questions can be answered using these data?

stimulus.description: Variables recorded for each of 300 households in a town.

options.text: What was the monthly electric bill for each of the households?
options.why: Asks for a listing of individual values rather than a question about a population that can be answered by summarizing and analyzing the data.

options.text: Would adding another resident to a household cause its monthly electric bill to increase?
options.why: A cause-and-effect question needs data from a randomized experiment, but these data were only recorded, not assigned.

options.text: Is there an association between the number of residents in a household and its monthly electric bill?
options.why: Uses only variables that were recorded and asks about a relationship that the recorded data can address.

options.text: Do households with a higher annual income have a larger monthly electric bill?
options.why: Needs a variable that was not recorded, so the data cannot answer it.

blueprint.subject: ap_statistics
blueprint.concept: Decide which investigative question the collected data can answer
student_thinking: Match the variables named in each question to the variables in the table
Reject questions that need uncollected variables, need random assignment for a cause-and-effect claim, or ask for individual values

key_conditions.condition: an investigative question must be answerable with the collected variables and the study design
key_conditions.evidence: the table lists every variable that was recorded and the stem says the data come from a survey

misconceptions.description: needs a variable that was not recorded
asks a cause-and-effect question of survey data
asks for a list of individual values

verification.independent_path: the variable names in each option are matched mechanically against the table and exactly one option uses only recorded variables and an association question

ap_statistics-m03.stem: A company claims that $80\%$ of its customers are satisfied. A consumer group suspects the true proportion is higher than the claim. Let $p$ be the proportion of all customers who are satisfied. Which of the following pairs of hypotheses should be tested?

options.why: The parameter is the proportion of all customers who are satisfied; the null hypothesis states the claimed value and the alternative matches the suspicion, which is one-sided.
Writes a two-sided alternative although the suspicion has a direction.
Puts the claim of the suspicion in the null hypothesis and an equal sign in the alternative, instead of an equal sign in the null.
Writes the hypotheses about a sample statistic, but hypotheses are always about the population parameter.

blueprint.subject: ap_statistics
blueprint.concept: Choose the null and alternative hypotheses from a scenario
student_thinking: Identify the population parameter and the claimed value that goes in the null hypothesis
Match the direction of the alternative hypothesis to the direction of the suspicion

key_conditions.condition: the null hypothesis states equality with the claimed value and the alternative reflects what is suspected
key_conditions.evidence: the stem states the claim and the direction of the suspicion in words

misconceptions.description: uses an alternative in the wrong direction
writes hypotheses about a sample statistic
swaps the roles of the two hypotheses

verification.independent_path: each option is built from a table of direction, parameter symbol and role of the equality, and only one row matches the scenario's claim and suspicion

ap_statistics-m04.stem: A coach wants to test whether the mean time for all of her runners to finish a mile is less than $7$ minutes, using the times of a random sample of $25$ runners. Which of the following procedures is appropriate?

options.text: A one-sample z-test for a population proportion
options.why: Chooses a one-sample z-test for a population proportion, but the scenario's data are measurements, not counts of a category.

options.text: A two-sample t-test for a difference in population means
options.why: Chooses a two-sample t-test for a difference in population means, but the number of samples does not fit the scenario.

options.text: A one-sample t-test for a population mean
options.why: The variables, the number of samples and the goal in the scenario match this procedure.

options.text: A matched-pairs t-test for a mean difference
options.why: Chooses a matched-pairs t-test for a mean difference, but the scenario's data are measurements, not counts of a category; the number of samples does not fit the scenario.

blueprint.subject: ap_statistics
blueprint.concept: Choose the statistical inference procedure that fits a scenario
student_thinking: Decide whether the data are categorical counts or measurements and whether the individuals are paired
Count the samples and decide whether the goal is an interval or a test, then match the procedure

key_conditions.condition: the type of variable, the number of samples, pairing and the goal determine the procedure
key_conditions.evidence: the scenario states the variable, the sampling and the goal

misconceptions.description: mixes up proportions and means
uses the wrong number of samples or ignores pairing
uses a test when an interval is needed or the reverse

verification.independent_path: a feature table (variable type, sample count, pairing, goal) is matched against each procedure and exactly one procedure matches the scenario

ap_statistics-m05.stem: A polling firm wants to estimate the proportion of all registered voters in a city who support a proposed park, using a random sample of $400$ voters. Which of the following procedures is appropriate?

options.text: A one-sample t-interval for a population mean
options.why: Chooses a one-sample t-interval for a population mean, but the scenario's data are counts of a category.

options.text: A chi-square test of independence
options.why: Chooses a chi-square test of independence, but the scenario's data are counts of a category; the scenario's goal is an interval, not a test.

options.text: A one-sample z-interval for a population proportion
options.why: The variables, the number of samples and the goal in the scenario match this procedure.

options.text: A two-sample z-test for a difference in population proportions
options.why: Chooses a two-sample z-test for a difference in population proportions, but the number of samples does not fit the scenario; the scenario's goal is an interval, not a test.

blueprint.subject: ap_statistics
blueprint.concept: Choose the statistical inference procedure that fits a scenario
student_thinking: Decide whether the data are categorical counts or measurements and whether the individuals are paired
Count the samples and decide whether the goal is an interval or a test, then match the procedure

key_conditions.condition: the type of variable, the number of samples, pairing and the goal determine the procedure
key_conditions.evidence: the scenario states the variable, the sampling and the goal

misconceptions.description: mixes up proportions and means
uses the wrong number of samples or ignores pairing
uses a test when an interval is needed or the reverse

verification.independent_path: a feature table (variable type, sample count, pairing, goal) is matched against each procedure and exactly one procedure matches the scenario

ap_statistics-m06.stem: An inspector tests whether the proportion of defective parts in a shipment exceeds the allowed limit, using the null hypothesis that the true proportion of defective parts is at most the allowed limit and the alternative hypothesis that the true proportion of defective parts is above the allowed limit. Which of the following describes a Type I error in this context?

options.text: The test leads to the decision to reject the shipment and the true proportion of defective parts is above the allowed limit
options.why: Describes a correct decision (rejecting a false null hypothesis), not an error.

options.text: The test does not lead to the decision to reject the shipment and the true proportion of defective parts is at most the allowed limit
options.why: Describes a correct decision (failing to reject a true null hypothesis), not an error.

options.text: The test leads to the decision to reject the shipment even though the true proportion of defective parts is at most the allowed limit
options.why: A Type I error is rejecting a null hypothesis that is true.

options.text: The test does not lead to the decision to reject the shipment even though the true proportion of defective parts is above the allowed limit
options.why: Describes a Type II error, mixing up the two types of error.

blueprint.subject: ap_statistics
blueprint.concept: Describe a Type I error in context
student_thinking: Recall that a Type I error rejects a true null hypothesis and a Type II error fails to reject a false null hypothesis
Translate the decision and the state of nature into the words of the scenario

key_conditions.condition: the type of error is determined by the true state of the null hypothesis and the decision
key_conditions.evidence: the stem states the null and alternative hypotheses and what rejecting leads to

misconceptions.description: swaps Type I and Type II
calls a correct decision an error
calls the other correct decision an error

verification.independent_path: the four options are the four cells of the truth-by-decision table; exactly one cell matches the requested error type

ap_statistics-m07.stem: The company wants a sample of $50$ employees from a list of $800$ in which every group of $50$ employees is equally likely to be chosen. The plan is to number the employees from $1$ to $800$ and use a random number generator to choose $50$ different numbers. Which of the following best describes this sampling method?

options.text: A convenience sample
options.why: Chooses whoever is easy to reach, which is likely to be biased and does not use random selection.

options.text: A cluster sample
options.why: Selects whole groups at random and surveys every member, which does not match a goal of spreading the sample across the list.

options.text: A simple random sample
options.why: This method matches the goal: number the employees from $1$ to $800$ and use a random number generator to choose $50$ different numbers.

options.text: A stratified random sample
options.why: Does not guarantee that each subgroup is represented in proportion; only random selection within each subgroup guarantees it.

blueprint.subject: ap_statistics
blueprint.concept: Justify a sampling method that fits a stated goal
student_thinking: Identify the goal stated in the scenario, such as representation of subgroups, cost of reaching whole groups or equal chance for every group of the chosen size
Match that goal and the described plan to the one sampling method that has this property

key_conditions.condition: each sampling method has a defining property that matches one goal
key_conditions.evidence: the stem states both the goal and the selection plan

misconceptions.description: names another random method
names a different random method
treats a convenience sample as random

verification.independent_path: a table of methods and defining properties is used and exactly one method has the property required by the stated goal

ap_statistics-m08.stem: In a company with $8000$ employees, a random sample of $60$ employees is used to test $H_0: p = 0.5$, where $p$ is the proportion of all employees who work remotely at least one day a week. A one-sample z-test for a proportion is planned. Which of the following statements about the conditions for this test is correct?

options.text: The $10\%$ condition is not satisfied
options.why: Claims the $10\%$ condition fails even though $60$ is less than $10\%$ of $8000$.

options.text: The large counts condition is not satisfied
options.why: Claims the large counts condition fails even though $np_0 = 30$ and $n(1-p_0) = 30$ are both at least $10$.

options.text: All three conditions are satisfied
options.why: Each condition is verified: the sample is random, $60 < 10\%$ of $8000$, and both expected counts are at least $10$.

options.text: The random condition is not satisfied
options.why: Claims the sample is not random even though the sample was selected at random.

blueprint.subject: ap_statistics
blueprint.concept: Verify the conditions for a one-sample z-test for a proportion
student_thinking: Check each condition separately: random selection, the 10 percent condition for independence and the large counts condition using the null value
Find the single condition that fails, or decide that all are met

key_conditions.condition: a z-test for a proportion needs random selection, a sample under 10 percent of the population and both np0 and n(1-p0) at least 10
key_conditions.evidence: the stem gives the sampling method, the sample and population sizes and the null value

misconceptions.description: says conditions are met when one fails
claims random fails
claims large counts fails

verification.independent_path: each condition is evaluated separately in code and exactly one statement agrees with all three evaluations

ap_statistics-m09.stem: A random sample of $45$ lengths, in centimeters, of fish caught in a lake is selected. The dotplot shown displays the sample data. The researcher plans to construct a $95\%$ confidence interval for the population mean using a t-procedure. Which of the following statements is correct?

options.text: A t-procedure is not reasonable because the population standard deviation is not known
options.why: A t-procedure is designed for an unknown population standard deviation, so this is not a reason to reject it.

options.text: A t-procedure is reasonable because t procedures work for any sample size and any shape
options.why: Believes the t-procedures work for any sample size and shape, but strong skewness or outliers in a small sample are a problem.

options.text: A t-procedure is reasonable because the sample size $45$ is at least $30$, so the sampling distribution of the sample mean is approximately normal
options.why: Since $45 \ge 30$ the Central Limit Theorem makes the sampling distribution of the mean approximately normal even though the sample is skewed.

options.text: A t-procedure is not reasonable because the dotplot is skewed
options.why: Ignores that a sample size of at least $30$ allows the procedure even when the sample is skewed.

blueprint.subject: ap_statistics
blueprint.concept: Verify the normality condition for a t-procedure from the sample size and a graph
student_thinking: Check the sample size: at least 30 allows the Central Limit Theorem to apply
For a smaller sample, read the dotplot for strong skewness or outliers before deciding

key_conditions.condition: a t-procedure for a mean is justified by n at least 30 or by a graph that shows no strong skewness or outliers
key_conditions.evidence: the stem gives the sample size and the dotplot shows the sample data

misconceptions.description: rejects a small symmetric sample
applies the Central Limit Theorem to a small sample
cites an unknown sigma as the problem

verification.independent_path: the sample is simulated and the skewness, interquartile outlier count and sample size are computed independently of the plotted counts; the case is accepted only if the rule agrees with the planned case

ap_statistics-m10.stem: A researcher compares the time to run a mile, in minutes, for athletes in two training programs, Program A and Program B, using independent random samples of $12$ and $14$ observations, respectively. The boxplots shown display the sample data. The researcher plans a two-sample t-interval for the difference in population means. Which statement about the normality condition is correct?

stimulus.description: Side-by-side boxplots for Program A and Program B

options.text: A two-sample t-procedure is not reasonable because a sample size is less than $30$ and the boxplot for Program B shows an outlier
options.why: With a sample size below $30$ an outlier in the boxplot for Program B is a problem for the normality condition.

options.text: A two-sample t-procedure is reasonable because the two boxplots have about the same spread
options.why: Equal spread is not the condition: the shapes of the two distributions must be checked, not their spreads.

options.text: A two-sample t-procedure is not reasonable because the two sample sizes are not equal
options.why: The sample sizes do not need to be equal for a two-sample t-procedure.

options.text: A two-sample t-procedure is reasonable because boxplots can never show a problem with the normality condition
options.why: Boxplots do display outliers, so they can show a problem with the normality condition.

blueprint.subject: ap_statistics
blueprint.concept: Verify the normality condition for a two-sample t-procedure from sample sizes and boxplots
student_thinking: Check each sample size: at least 30 allows the Central Limit Theorem to apply
For smaller samples, read each boxplot for outliers or strong skewness before deciding

key_conditions.condition: a two-sample t-procedure is justified when both samples are at least 30 or the graphs show no strong skewness or outliers
key_conditions.evidence: the stem gives both sample sizes and the boxplots show the sample data

misconceptions.description: treats unequal sample sizes as a problem
rejects every small sample regardless of the graphs
believes the boxplot cannot show a problem

verification.independent_path: the outlier rule is applied again to the plotted five-number summaries, and the decision rule is evaluated separately from the planned case

ap_statistics-m11.stem: A study compares the proportion of patients who attend their scheduled appointment for a group using a new reminder text message (Reminder group) and a comparison group (Control group), using independent random samples of $274$ and $183$ patients, and the conditions for inference are met. A $95\%$ confidence interval for $p_1 - p_2$ is $(-0.061,\ 0.115)$, where $p_1$ is the proportion for the reminder group and $p_2$ is the proportion for the control group. Which of the following claims is justified by the interval?

options.text: There is a $95\%$ probability that the difference in sample proportions lies in the interval $(-0.061,\ 0.115)$
options.why: Interprets the confidence level as a probability about the sample statistic instead of describing the method.

options.text: There is convincing evidence that the proportion of patients who attend their scheduled appointment is greater for the reminder group than for the control group
options.why: Claims a positive difference even though the interval includes $0$.

options.text: The interval contains $0$, so there is convincing evidence that the two population proportions are equal
options.why: Treats an interval that contains $0$ as proof that the proportions are equal instead of as a lack of evidence for a difference.

options.text: There is not convincing evidence of a difference in the proportions of patients who attend their scheduled appointment between the two groups
options.why: The interval $(-0.061,\ 0.115)$ contains $0$, so $0$ is a plausible value for the difference and a difference is not supported.

blueprint.subject: ap_statistics
blueprint.concept: Justify a claim about a difference of proportions from a confidence interval
student_thinking: Check whether zero is inside the interval for the difference
If zero is outside, use the sign of the interval to decide which population proportion is larger

key_conditions.condition: an interval for a difference that excludes 0 supports a difference in the direction of its sign, and an interval containing 0 does not
key_conditions.evidence: the stem gives the interval, defines p1 and p2 and says the conditions are met

misconceptions.description: treats inclusion of zero as proof of no difference
reverses the direction of the difference
gives a probability interpretation of the confidence level

verification.independent_path: the interval is recomputed from counts with z* found by bisection on the normal cdf and the claim is derived from the sign pattern of the endpoints

ap_statistics-m12.stem: A least-squares regression line is used to predict exam score, in points, from the number of hours a student studied. The computer output shown is for the regression. For one student with hours equal to $4$, the actual score is $58.6$. What is the residual for this student? Round to one decimal place.

stimulus.description: Computer output for a least-squares regression

options.why: Subtracts in the wrong order (predicted minus observed), which reverses the sign of the residual.
Uses the slope as the intercept and the intercept as the slope when computing the predicted value.
The predicted value is $\hat y = 43.1 + (5.37)(4) \approx 64.58$, and the residual is observed minus predicted, $58.6 - 64.58 \approx -6.0$.
Leaves out the intercept and predicts with the slope times $x$ alone.

blueprint.subject: ap_statistics
blueprint.concept: Compute a residual from regression computer output
student_thinking: Read the intercept and the slope from the Coef column of the output
Compute the predicted value and subtract it from the observed value, in that order

key_conditions.condition: a residual is the observed response minus the value predicted by the least-squares line
key_conditions.evidence: the output gives the coefficients and the stem gives the x value and the observed y

misconceptions.description: subtracts in the wrong order
swaps slope and intercept
leaves out the intercept

verification.independent_path: the residual is recomputed from the coefficients and checked against the side of the line (above or below) on which the observed point lies

ap_statistics-m13.stem: A least-squares regression line is used to describe the relationship between the number of hours of practice per week and a musician's performance score. The relationship is positive, and the coefficient of determination is $r^2 = 0.64$. Which of the following is the correct interpretation of $r^2$?

options.text: Performance score increases by $64\%$ for each one-unit increase in practice time
options.why: Confuses $r^2$ with the slope and interprets it as a percent change in the response.

options.text: About $64\%$ of the points in the scatterplot lie exactly on the least-squares line
options.why: Misreads $r^2$ as the percent of data points that fall on the regression line.

options.text: About $64\%$ of the variation in performance score is accounted for by the linear relationship with practice time
options.why: $r^2 = 0.64$ is the proportion of the variation in the response that is explained by the linear relationship with the explanatory variable.

options.text: The correlation between practice time and performance score is $0.64$
options.why: Confuses $r^2$ with the correlation coefficient $r$: the correlation here is the square root of $r^2$ with the sign of the slope.

blueprint.subject: ap_statistics
blueprint.concept: Interpret the coefficient of determination in context
student_thinking: Recall that r squared is the proportion of the variation in the response accounted for by the linear relationship with the explanatory variable
Reject options that treat r squared as a percent of points on the line, a slope or the correlation

key_conditions.condition: r squared is the proportion of variation in y explained by the linear relationship with x
key_conditions.evidence: the stem gives r squared and the direction of the association

misconceptions.description: reads r squared as points on the line
reads r squared as a slope
confuses r squared with r

verification.independent_path: r squared is checked as the square of a correlation r whose sign matches the described direction, and the sentences are generated from a fixed set of interpretations

ap_statistics-m14.stem: The boxplots shown display test scores, in points, for Class A and Class B. Which of the following statements is correct?

stimulus.description: Side-by-side boxplots of test scores, in points

options.text: The third quartile of Class A is greater than the third quartile of Class B
options.why: The right edge of the box for the other class is farther right, so this comparison is reversed.

options.text: The interquartile range of Class A is greater than the interquartile range of Class B
options.why: This comparison is true for the plotted five-number summaries.

options.text: The maximum of Class A is greater than the maximum of Class B
options.why: The upper whisker of the other class extends farther right, so this comparison is reversed.

options.text: The median of Class A is greater than the median of Class B
options.why: The line inside the box of the other class is higher, so this comparison of medians is reversed.

blueprint.subject: ap_statistics
blueprint.concept: Compare two distributions displayed in boxplots
student_thinking: Read the median, the quartiles and the whisker ends for each group from the boxplot
Evaluate each statement about center, spread or extremes and keep the one that matches the plotted values

key_conditions.condition: a boxplot shows the minimum, the quartiles, the median and the maximum
key_conditions.evidence: the boxplots show the five-number summaries of both groups with no outliers

misconceptions.description: reverses a comparison of medians
reverses a comparison of spreads
misreads a whisker end

verification.independent_path: each statement is evaluated against the plotted five-number summaries and exactly one of the four chosen statements is true

ap_statistics-m15.stem: The table shown summarizes the responses of $180$ students. One student is selected at random. Let $A$ be the event that the student is a freshman and let $B$ be the event that the student has a job. Which of the following statements is correct? Round probabilities to three decimal places.

stimulus.description: Two-way table of grade level and response

options.text: The events are not independent because they can both occur at the same time
options.why: Confuses independent events with mutually exclusive events.

options.text: The events are not independent because the number of students in each cell is not the same
options.why: Thinks independence requires equal cell counts instead of equal conditional probabilities.

options.text: The events are not independent because $P(A \text{ and } B) \approx 0.111$ is not equal to $P(A) = 0.333$
options.why: Compares the joint probability with $P(A)$ instead of with $P(A)\cdot P(B)$.

options.text: The events are independent because $P(A\mid B) = P(A) = 0.333$
options.why: Independent events satisfy $P(A\mid B)=P(A)$; the table gives the counts needed to compare the two.

blueprint.subject: ap_statistics
blueprint.concept: Decide whether two events are independent from a two-way table
student_thinking: Find P(A) and the conditional probability P(A given B) from the table
Compare the two: events are independent only when they are equal

key_conditions.condition: events A and B are independent exactly when P(A given B) equals P(A)

misconceptions.description: thinks independence needs equal counts
confuses independence with mutual exclusivity
compares the wrong probabilities

verification.independent_path: the table is expanded into individual records and P(A given B) and P(A) are found by enumeration, independent of the cell-ratio calculation
